lessons.title: Greetings And Polite Openers
lessons.learningObjective: memakai sapaan dasar dan formula pembuka interaksi singkat.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces expressions used to open short interactions in Japanese. Your goal is to choose a greeting that fits the time and relationship, then use a natural formula when meeting someone for the first time or politely getting someone's attention.

contentBlocks.title: Greetings By Time Of Day
contentBlocks.body: Basic greetings change with the time of day. Use おはよう in the morning with friends or family, おはようございます in polite morning situations, こんにちは during the day, and こんばんは in the evening. In こんにちは and こんばんは, the final kana is written は but pronounced wa.

contentBlocks.title: Meeting Someone For The First Time
contentBlocks.body: Start a first meeting with はじめまして. You can then say your name and close the introduction with よろしくおねがいします. A simple pattern is: はじめまして。アリです。よろしくおねがいします。 The whole exchange sounds natural as one short introduction rather than as separate vocabulary items.

contentBlocks.title: Casual And Polite Choices
contentBlocks.body: The relationship between speakers affects the expression you choose. おはよう is casual, while おはようございます is safer with teachers, coworkers, customers, or people you do not know well. よろしくおねがいします is also more complete and polite than the shorter よろしく.

contentBlocks.title: Polite Ways To Begin A Question Or Visit
contentBlocks.body: Japanese often uses a short expression before the main message. Say すみません to politely get someone's attention before asking a question. Say しつれいします when entering a teacher's room, office, or another space where you should acknowledge that you are interrupting.

contentBlocks.title: A Natural Mini Dialogue
contentBlocks.body: A short first meeting can sound like this: A: はじめまして。リナです。よろしくおねがいします。 B: ケンです。こちらこそ、よろしくおねがいします。 The phrase こちらこそ means roughly “likewise” and shows that the second speaker returns the same polite feeling.

lessons.title: Copula Affirmative And Questions
lessons.learningObjective: membuat kalimat nominal sangat dasar tentang identitas diri dan orang lain.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson helps you build very basic noun sentences for introductions and identity. You will learn how to say that someone is a student, teacher, or another role, how to turn that statement into a polite question, and how the casual ending だ differs from polite です.

content.title: Polite Statements With です
content.body: A beginner-friendly identification pattern is A は B です. Depending on the context, the same pattern may be translated with “am,” “is,” or “are.” The ending です makes the statement polite, so it works well when meeting someone, speaking to a teacher, or talking with a person you do not know well.

content.POLITE:
[Topic] + は + Noun + です
Name + です

content.japaneseSentence: わたしは ミナです。
content.englishTranslation: I am Mina.

content.title: Asking A Polite Question With か
content.body: To turn a polite noun sentence into a yes-or-no question, add か after です: A は B ですか. In writing, Japanese often ends this kind of question with 。, although ？ is also common in informal modern writing.

content.POLITE:
[Topic] + は + Noun + ですか
Noun + ですか

content.japaneseSentence: 田中さんは 先生ですか。
content.englishTranslation: Is Mr. Tanaka a teacher?

content.title: Keep Answers Natural And Short
content.body: When the topic is already clear, Japanese often leaves it out. After someone asks マリアさんは 学生ですか, a natural answer is simply はい、学生です. You do not need to repeat マリアさんは unless it helps clarify who you mean.

content.title: Casual Statements With だ
content.body: The plain or casual counterpart of です is だ. You may hear it between close friends, family members, or in casual narration. For example, ぼくは 学生だ means “I am a student” in a casual tone. Avoid using だ when a polite interaction calls for です.

content.japaneseSentence: ぼくは 大学生だ。
content.englishTranslation: I am a university student.

content.title: Choose The Ending By Situation
content.body: Use です for a polite statement, ですか for a polite question, and だ for a casual statement. The noun itself does not change; the ending shows whether you are making a statement or asking a question, and whether the tone is polite or casual.

lessons.learningObjective: menolak atau merujuk identitas/keadaan nominal di waktu lampau.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson extends basic noun sentences so you can say that someone or something is not a certain identity, describe what someone or something was, and say what it was not. The noun stays the same; the copula ending changes to show negation and past time.

content.title: Polite Negative With ではありません
content.body: To make a polite noun sentence negative, replace です with ではありません. The basic pattern is A は B ではありません, meaning “A is not B.” This form works well in introductions, corrections, and other polite situations.

content.POLITE:
[Topic] + は + Noun + ではありません
[Topic] + は + Noun + じゃありません

content.japaneseSentence: わたしは 先生ではありません。学生です。
content.englishTranslation: I am not a teacher. I am a student.

content.title: Conversational Polite Negative With じゃありません
content.body: In everyday conversation, ではありません is often shortened to じゃありません. Both are polite negatives, but ではありません sounds more formal, while じゃありません feels more conversational. Choose one form and keep it together as a complete ending.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：田中さんは 医者ですか。
B：いいえ、医者じゃありません。
content.englishTranslation:
A: Is Mr. Tanaka a doctor?
B: No, he is not a doctor.

content.title: Polite Past With でした
content.body: To describe a past identity or past noun state politely, replace です with でした. Use the pattern A は B でした. Do not say ですでした; でした already carries the polite past meaning.

content.POLITE: [Topic] + は + Noun + でした

content.japaneseSentence: 去年、わたしは 高校生でした。
content.englishTranslation: Last year, I was a high school student.

content.title: Polite Negative Past
content.body: To say that a noun identity or state was not true in the past, use ではありませんでした. In conversational polite speech, you may also hear じゃありませんでした. The ending may look long, but it works as one unit: A は B ではありませんでした.

content.POLITE:
[Topic] + は + Noun + ではありませんでした
[Topic] + は + Noun + じゃありませんでした

content.japaneseSentence: きのうは 休みではありませんでした。
content.englishTranslation: Yesterday was not a day off.

content.title: Use Time Context To Choose The Form
content.body: Words such as 今 (now), きのう (yesterday), 去年 (last year), and 前 (before) help you choose the ending. Use ではありません or じゃありません for a present negative, でした for a polite past statement, and ではありませんでした or じゃありませんでした for a polite negative past statement.

lessons.title: Belonging Role And Basic Preference
lessons.learningObjective: menyebut peran, afiliasi, dan preferensi sederhana dalam konteks perkenalan.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson helps you add useful personal details to a basic introduction. You will name roles and affiliations, show that you share something with another person using も, and talk about simple likes or dislikes with 好きです and 嫌いです.

contentBlocks.title: Talking About Roles And Identity
contentBlocks.body: Use the familiar pattern A は B です to state a role, identity, or affiliation. Common words include 学生（がくせい） “student,” 大学生（だいがくせい） “university student,” 先生（せんせい） “teacher,” 会社員（かいしゃいん） “company employee,” and エンジニア “engineer.” Nationality words often use a country name followed by 人（じん）, as in インドネシア人.

content.japaneseSentence: わたしは大学生です。兄はエンジニアです。
content.englishTranslation: I am a university student. My older brother is an engineer.

contentBlocks.title: Saying “Also” With も
contentBlocks.body: The particle も means “also” or “too.” It usually replaces は when the new topic shares the same role, identity, or situation: ミナさんは学生です。わたしも学生です。 means “Mina is a student. I am also a student.” Do not combine them as はも.

content.STANDARD:
Person + も + Role + だ
Person + も + Thing + が + 好きだ / 嫌いだ
content.POLITE:
Person + も + Role + です
Person + も + Thing + が + 好きです / 嫌いです

content.japaneseSentence: アリさんは会社員です。サラさんも会社員です。
content.englishTranslation: Ali is a company employee. Sara is also a company employee.

contentBlocks.title: Basic Likes And Dislikes
contentBlocks.body: To state a basic preference, use A は B が好きです for “A likes B” and A は B が嫌いです for “A dislikes B.” The person is marked as the topic with は, while the liked or disliked thing is commonly marked with が. 嫌いです is fairly direct, so this lesson uses it mainly to teach the core contrast with 好きです.

content.STANDARD:
Person + は + Thing + が好きだ
Person + は + Thing + が嫌いだ
content.POLITE:
Person + は + Thing + が好きです
Person + は + Thing + が嫌いです

content.japaneseSentence: わたしは日本語が好きです。妹は魚が嫌いです。
content.englishTranslation: I like Japanese. My younger sister dislikes fish.

contentBlocks.title: Sharing The Same Preference
contentBlocks.body: You can also use も when two people share a preference. For example, ケンさんはコーヒーが好きです。わたしもコーヒーが好きです。 means “Ken likes coffee. I like coffee too.” At this stage, keep the repeated noun in the sentence so the meaning stays clear.

contentBlocks.title: Building A More Complete Introduction
contentBlocks.body: A short introduction can now include several connected facts: はじめまして。リナです。大学生です。日本語が好きです。 Another person can respond with shared information, such as わたしも大学生です。わたしも日本語が好きです。 These small additions make an introduction feel more personal without requiring a long sentence.

lessons.title: KO SO A DO Pronouns
lessons.learningObjective: menunjuk benda dengan referensi dekat-pendengar-jauh.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces the four basic Japanese pronouns used to point to things: これ, それ, あれ, and どれ. The right choice depends on where the object is in relation to the speaker and listener.

contentBlocks.title: The Ko-So-A-Do Distance System
contentBlocks.body: The first sound gives you a useful distance clue. The こ series points near the speaker, the そ series points near the listener, the あ series points away from both people, and the ど series asks a question. For standalone things, these become これ, それ, あれ, and どれ.

contentBlocks.title: これ: Near The Speaker
contentBlocks.body: Use これ for an object close to you, the speaker. You might use it while holding an item or pointing to something on your side of a table. A simple pattern is これは + noun + です, meaning “This is ...”.

content.japaneseSentence: これはノートです。
content.englishTranslation: This is a notebook.

contentBlocks.title: それ: Near The Listener
contentBlocks.body: Use それ for an object close to the listener. This means the same item can be これ for one person and それ for the other. If you hold up a notebook and ask what it is, the other person can answer with それ.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「これはなんですか。」

B：「それはじしょです。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “What is this?”

B: “That is a dictionary.”

contentBlocks.title: あれ: Far From Both People
contentBlocks.body: Use あれ when the object is away from both the speaker and the listener. It often appears when both people look toward the same distant object, such as a bag near the door or an umbrella across the room.

content.japaneseSentence: あれは先生のかばんです。
content.englishTranslation: That over there is the teacher’s bag.

contentBlocks.title: どれ: Which One?
contentBlocks.body: Use どれ to ask “which one?” when choosing from several visible things. A useful pattern is noun + はどれですか. For example, ゆきさんのかさはどれですか asks which umbrella belongs to Yuki.

contentBlocks.title: These Pronouns Stand Alone
contentBlocks.body: これ, それ, あれ, and どれ replace a noun, so do not place a noun directly after them. Say これはほんです, not これほん. The forms that come directly before nouns—such as “this book”—belong to the next lesson.

lessons.title: KO SO A DO Modifiers
lessons.learningObjective: memodifikasi noun dengan referensi `this/that/which`.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces この, その, あの, and どの. These words point to a specific person, place, or thing, but unlike これ or それ, they must be followed directly by a noun.

contentBlocks.title: Pronoun Or Noun Modifier?
contentBlocks.body: Use これ・それ・あれ・どれ when the pointing word stands by itself. Use この・その・あの・どの when you immediately name the noun. For example, これは本です means “This is a book,” while この本はおもしろいです means “This book is interesting.”

content.ALL:
この + Noun — this noun near the speaker
その + Noun — that noun near the listener
あの + Noun — that noun away from both people
どの + Noun — which noun

contentBlocks.title: この And その
contentBlocks.body: Use この + noun for something close to the current speaker. Use その + noun for something close to the listener. Because the correct word depends on who is speaking, the same object may be called この本 by one person and その本 by the other.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「この本はわたしのです。」

B：「その本は日本語の本ですか。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “This book is mine.”

B: “Is that book a Japanese-language book?”

contentBlocks.title: あの For Something Far Away
contentBlocks.body: Use あの + noun when the person or thing is away from both the speaker and the listener. The speakers may be looking across a room, across a street, or toward another area that both understand from the situation.

content.japaneseSentence: あの人は山田先生です。
content.englishTranslation: That person over there is Mr. Yamada.

contentBlocks.title: どの For Choosing One
contentBlocks.body: Use どの + noun when asking which member of a visible or understood group is meant. The noun cannot be omitted in this pattern: say どのかばんですか for “Which bag is it?” If you do not say the noun, use the standalone pronoun どれですか instead.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「どのかさが佐藤さんのですか。」

B：「あの黒いかさです。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Which umbrella is Ms. Sato’s?”

B: “It is that black umbrella over there.”

contentBlocks.title: Avoid A Common Mix-Up
contentBlocks.body: Do not place a noun directly after これ・それ・あれ・どれ. Forms such as これ本 and どれ本 are incorrect. Use この本 and どの本, or let the pronoun stand alone as これは… and どれですか.

lessons.title: Place Reference And Location Questions
lessons.learningObjective: menanyakan dan menyebut lokasi sangat dasar.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces the place-reference words ここ, そこ, あそこ, and どこ. You will use them to point out a location, ask where something is, and understand how the correct word changes with the speaker's position.

contentBlocks.title: Three Location Zones
contentBlocks.body: Japanese divides locations into three simple zones. ここ means “here,” close to the speaker. そこ means “there,” usually close to the listener. あそこ means “over there,” away from both the speaker and the listener.

content.ALL:
ここ — here, near the speaker
そこ — there, near the listener
あそこ — over there, away from both people

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「トイレはどこですか。」

B：「あそこです。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Where is the restroom?”

B: “It is over there.”

contentBlocks.title: The Speaker's Position Matters
contentBlocks.body: The same place can be described differently after the speaker changes. A person standing beside the reception desk may say ここです. Someone across from that person may refer to the same desk as そこです. Always imagine where the current speaker and listener are standing.

contentBlocks.title: Asking Where Something Is
contentBlocks.body: Use どこ when the location is unknown. A very useful pattern is Noun は どこですか, meaning “Where is the noun?” The answer can be ここです, そこです, or あそこです.

content.ALL:
Noun + は + どこ + ですか
ここ / そこ / あそこ + です

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「田中先生の部屋はどこですか。」

B：「そこです。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Where is Mr. Tanaka's room?”

B: “It is there.”

contentBlocks.title: Short And Natural Answers
contentBlocks.body: When the topic is already clear, a short answer such as ここです or あそこです is natural. You do not need to repeat the place name in every reply. In conversation, pointing or shared visual context often makes the short answer clear.

contentBlocks.title: Avoid Common Mix-Ups
contentBlocks.body: Do not use これ・それ・あれ when you mean a location; those forms point to things. Use ここ・そこ・あそこ for places. Also remember that どこ asks “where,” while どれ asks “which one.”

lessons.title: Choice And Person Reference
lessons.learningObjective: menanyakan orang, pilihan benda, dan kepemilikan sederhana.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson helps you ask about a person and choose one item from a group. You will use だれ for “who,” どれ for “which one,” and どの before a noun. You will also meet だれの when asking who owns something.

contentBlocks.title: Asking Who A Person Is
contentBlocks.body: Use だれ when you do not know a person's identity. A common pattern is Person or role は だれですか. For example, you can ask who a teacher, group leader, or person in a photograph is.

content.ALL:
Noun + は + だれ + ですか
だれ + ですか

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「クラスの先生はだれですか。」

B：「田中先生です。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Who is the class teacher?”

B: “It is Mr. Tanaka.”

contentBlocks.title: Asking Who Owns Something
contentBlocks.body: Add の after だれ to ask about ownership. The pattern だれの + noun means “whose noun.” For example, だれのかばんですか means “Whose bag is it?”

content.ALL:
だれ + の + Noun + ですか
Noun + は + だれ + の + ですか

contentBlocks.title: Choosing One With どれ
contentBlocks.body: Use どれ when several things are visible or already understood and you want to ask “which one?” Because どれ stands on its own, do not place a noun directly after it. A useful pattern is Noun は どれですか.

content.ALL:
Noun + は + どれ + ですか
どれ + にしますか

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「マリアさんのかさはどれですか。」

B：「青いかさです。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Which one is Maria's umbrella?”

B: “It is the blue umbrella.”

contentBlocks.title: Using どの Before A Noun
contentBlocks.body: Use どの when the noun still needs to be named. It must come directly before a noun, as in どの本 (“which book”) or どの人 (“which person”). Unlike どれ, どの cannot stand alone.

content.ALL:
どの + Noun + ですか
どの + Noun + を + Verb
Noun + は + どの + Noun + ですか

content.japaneseSentence:
A：「田中先生はどの人ですか。」

B：「めがねの人です。」
content.englishTranslation:
A: “Which person is Mr. Tanaka?”

B: “It is the person with glasses.”

contentBlocks.title: どれ Or どの?
contentBlocks.body: Choose どれ when the expression ends with “which one,” such as あなたの本はどれですか. Choose どの when a noun follows immediately, such as どの本ですか. A quick check is simple: if you say the noun after the question word, use どの.

units.title: Core Particles And Sentence Order
units.description: Mengunci pola topik, subjek, objek, kepemilikan, dan penyusunan kalimat pendek yang stabil. Unit ini adalah fondasi struktural untuk hampir semua lesson sesudahnya.

lessons.title: Topic Subject And Possession
lessons.learningObjective: membedakan topik, subjek, dan relasi kepemilikan sederhana.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces three small particles that do a lot of work in Japanese: は, が, and の. You will learn how to set the topic of a sentence, identify its subject, and connect two nouns to show ownership or another close relationship.

contentBlocks.title: Setting The Topic With は
contentBlocks.body: The particle は introduces what the sentence is about. A useful way to feel its role is “as for ...”. In 私は学生です, 私 is the topic and 学生です is the comment about that topic. When は is used as a particle, it is written は but pronounced wa.

content.ALL:
Noun / noun phrase + は + comment

は sets the noun before it as the topic of the sentence.

content.japaneseSentence: 私は学生です。
content.englishTranslation: I am a student.

contentBlocks.title: Identifying The Subject With が
contentBlocks.body: The particle が marks the person or thing that directly has the identity, quality, or state being described. It is especially common when the sentence identifies new or unknown information. Question words such as 誰 and どの人 normally take が when they ask who the subject is.

content.ALL:
Noun / question word + が + description or identification

が highlights the subject that answers “who?” or “what?”.

content.japaneseSentence: 誰が先生ですか。田中さんが先生です。
content.englishTranslation: Who is the teacher? Mr. Tanaka is the teacher.

contentBlocks.title: Using は And が In The Same Sentence
contentBlocks.body: は and が can appear in the same sentence because they have different jobs. In 私は日本語が好きです, 私は sets the broader topic, while 日本語が identifies what is liked. At this level, focus on the practical pattern: the topic gives the frame, and が marks the specific person or thing connected to the description.

contentBlocks.title: Connecting Nouns With の
contentBlocks.body: The particle の connects one noun to another. The first noun describes the second noun by showing an owner, group, type, origin, or other relationship. ミナさんの本 means “Mina's book”, while 日本語の先生 means “a Japanese-language teacher”. The main noun always comes after の.

content.ALL:
Noun 1 + の + Noun 2

Noun 1 identifies the owner, group, type, or relationship of Noun 2.

content.japaneseSentence: これはミナさんの本です。
content.englishTranslation: This is Mina's book.

contentBlocks.title: A Practical Way To Choose
contentBlocks.body: Choose は when you are setting or contrasting the topic. Choose が when you are identifying the subject, especially after a question word or when answering who or what fits the description. Choose の when two nouns need to be connected. These are practical starting rules; later lessons will show more situations where the speaker's focus changes the choice between は and が.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson helps you build short action sentences with four useful particle functions. You will use を to mark the object of an action, と to join a complete pair or list, と to show who does an action with you, and や to give a few examples from a larger list.

contentBlocks.title: Marking The Object With を
contentBlocks.body: The particle を marks the noun directly affected by an action. In パンを食べます, bread is the thing being eaten. In 本を読みます, the book is the thing being read. Although the kana is written を, the particle is normally pronounced o.

content.ALL:
Noun + を + action verb

The noun before を is the object directly affected by the action.

content.japaneseSentence: 毎朝、パンを食べます。
content.englishTranslation: I eat bread every morning.

contentBlocks.title: Joining A Complete List With と
contentBlocks.body: Place と between nouns when you mean “and” and present them as a complete pair or list for the current sentence. パンとたまご means “bread and eggs”. After the nouns are joined, another particle can mark the whole group, as in パンとたまごを食べます.

content.ALL:
Noun 1 + と + Noun 2

Use this pattern to join the nouns as a complete pair or list in the sentence.

content.englishTranslation: I eat bread and eggs in the morning.

contentBlocks.title: Doing Something With Someone
contentBlocks.body: When a person or animal comes before と and the phrase connects to an action, と can mean “with”. In 友達と映画を見ます, the friend is the companion who watches the movie together with the speaker. The particle still links two participants, but its role is different from simply joining two nouns in a list.

content.ALL:
Person / animal + と + action verb

The noun before と is the companion who participates in the action.

content.englishTranslation: On Sunday, I will watch a movie with a friend.

contentBlocks.title: Giving Examples With や
contentBlocks.body: Use や when you mention some examples but do not give the whole list. パンや果物 means “bread, fruit, and things like that”. The word など, meaning “and so on” or “such as”, often appears after the final example and makes the open-ended meaning especially clear.

content.ALL:
Noun 1 + や + Noun 2 + (など)

Use this pattern to give examples from a larger list rather than naming every item.

content.englishTranslation: At the supermarket, I buy bread, fruit, and other things.

contentBlocks.title: Choosing Between と And や
contentBlocks.body: Use と when the named items form the complete list you want to present. Use や when the named items are only examples. 本とノートを買いました presents books and notebooks as the listed purchases, while 本やノートなどを買いました suggests that other things were bought too.

contentBlocks.title: Putting The Pieces Together
contentBlocks.body: A useful action-sentence pattern is Topic は + companion と + object を + verb. For example, 私は妹とケーキを食べます means “I eat cake with my younger sister.” A noun pair or loose list can also fill the object position: パンとたまごを食べます or パンや果物などを買います.

lessons.learningObjective: menandai lokasi aksi, tujuan, waktu, asal, dan batas sederhana.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces five particles that place an action in space or time. You will use に for a specific time or destination, で for the place or means of an action, へ for direction, から for a starting point, and まで for an ending point.

contentBlocks.title: Specific Times And Destinations With に
contentBlocks.body: The particle に commonly marks a specific time when an action happens. For example, 七時に起きます means “I wake up at seven.” It can also mark the destination of movement, as in 学校に行きます. With relative time words such as 今日, 明日, and 毎日, に is usually not needed.

content.ALL:
Specific time + に + action

Destination + に + movement verb

content.japaneseSentence: 毎朝、七時に起きます。
content.englishTranslation: I wake up at seven every morning.

contentBlocks.title: The Place Or Means Of An Action With で
contentBlocks.body: Use で to mark where an action takes place. In 図書館で勉強します, the library is the place where studying happens. The same particle can mark the means or method used for an action, as in バスで学校へ行きます or はしで食べます.

content.ALL:
Place + で + action

Means / method + で + action

content.japaneseSentence: カフェで日本語を勉強します。
content.englishTranslation: I study Japanese at a café.

contentBlocks.title: Showing Direction With へ
contentBlocks.body: The particle へ points toward a direction or destination. It is written へ but pronounced e when used as a particle. In movement sentences, へ often feels slightly more directional than に. A common expression is こちらへどうぞ, meaning “This way, please.”

content.ALL:
Direction / destination + へ + movement verb

こちらへどうぞ = This way, please.

content.japaneseSentence: 来月、日本へ行きます。
content.englishTranslation: I will go to Japan next month.

contentBlocks.title: Starting Points With から
contentBlocks.body: The particle から marks where or when something starts. For a place, インドネシアから来ました means “I came from Indonesia.” For time, 九時から働きます means “I work from nine.”

content.ALL:
Starting place / time + から

から marks the origin or beginning of a range.

content.japaneseSentence: 授業は九時からです。
content.englishTranslation: Class starts at nine.

contentBlocks.title: Ending Points With まで
contentBlocks.body: The particle まで marks the point where a movement, action, or time range ends. 駅まで歩きます means “I walk as far as the station,” and 五時まで働きます means “I work until five.” It often appears with から to show a full range.

content.ALL:
Ending place / time + まで

Starting point + から + ending point + まで

content.japaneseSentence: 図書館は朝九時から午後六時までです。
content.englishTranslation: The library is open from 9:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m.

contentBlocks.title: Choosing The Right Particle
contentBlocks.body: Ask what relationship the noun has with the action. Use に for a specific time or destination, で for the place where an action happens or the means used, へ when direction is the main idea, から for the starting point, and まで for the ending point. A sentence can contain several of them because each particle marks a different role.

lessons.title: Sentence Ending And Basic Quoting
lessons.learningObjective: memperhalus kalimat pendek dengan sentence ending dan kutipan ringan.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson Focus
contentBlocks.body: This lesson introduces three expressions that make short conversations sound more natural. Use ね when inviting the listener to agree or share a reaction, よ when giving information or emphasizing something the listener may not know, and って when casually repeating or quoting what someone said.

contentBlocks.title: Sharing A Reaction With ね
contentBlocks.body: Add ね at the end of a sentence when you expect the listener to recognize, confirm, or share the same feeling. 今日は暑いですね sounds like “It is hot today, isn't it?” The speaker is not simply delivering information; the speaker is opening space for agreement.

content.ALL:
Sentence + ね

Use ね to seek agreement, confirmation, or a shared reaction from the listener.

content.japaneseSentence: この公園は静かですね。
content.englishTranslation: This park is quiet, isn't it?

contentBlocks.title: Giving Information With よ
contentBlocks.body: Add よ when telling the listener something important, correcting an assumption, or drawing attention to information they may not know. For example, バスはもう来ましたよ can alert someone that the bus has already arrived. The tone can be friendly, but it is more informative or assertive than ね.

content.ALL:
Sentence + よ

Use よ to provide information, give a reminder, or emphasize a point for the listener.

content.japaneseSentence: 駅はあちらですよ。
content.englishTranslation: The station is over there.

contentBlocks.title: Choosing Between ね And よ
contentBlocks.body: The same basic sentence can feel different depending on the ending. きれいですね invites the listener to share the observation: “It is beautiful, isn't it?” きれいですよ presents the beauty as information or reassurance: “It is beautiful, you know.” Choose the ending based on what you are doing in the conversation, not only on the dictionary meaning of the sentence.

contentBlocks.title: Casually Repeating Speech With って
contentBlocks.body: The expression って can mark quoted words in casual conversation. It often works like a conversational version of the quotation particle と. In ミナさんは「少し遅れます」って言っていました, the words before って are what Mina said. In a short reply, the reporting verb may be omitted when the meaning is already clear.

content.ALL:
Quoted words + って + 言いました / 言っていました

In casual conversation, the reporting verb may be omitted: Quoted words + って.

content.japaneseSentence: ユキさんは「明日行きます」って言っていました。
content.englishTranslation: Yuki said, “I will go tomorrow.”

contentBlocks.title: Short Quoted Replies
contentBlocks.body: When someone asks what another person said, a short answer can end in って. For example: A: 先生は何と言っていましたか。 B: 「明日は休みです」って。 The full meaning is understood as “The teacher said that tomorrow is a day off.” This shortened pattern is conversational, so use it mainly in informal speech.

contentBlocks.title: A Simple Conversation Strategy
contentBlocks.body: Before choosing an ending, ask what the speaker is trying to do. Use ね to connect with the listener through shared knowledge or feeling. Use よ to deliver or emphasize useful information. Use って when the sentence repeats someone else's words. These small choices help a basic sentence function naturally inside a real conversation.

lessons.title: Polite Verb Basics
lessons.learningObjective: mengenali bentuk non-past sopan untuk rutinitas sehari-hari.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson introduces the polite non-past verb form used for everyday routines, general actions, and simple future plans. You will practice recognizing sentences that end in ます, changing them to polite negative sentences with ません, and asking natural questions with ますか.

content.title: Verbs Close Action Sentences
content.body: In a basic Japanese action sentence, the verb normally comes at the end. Details such as the topic, time, place, destination, or object appear before it. The final verb tells the listener what happens, so listen or read all the way to the end before deciding whether the sentence is affirmative, negative, or a question.

content.ALL:
Topic / Time / Place / Object + Non-past verb
Non-past verb = a routine, a general action, or a future action depending on the time expression and context

content.japaneseSentence: 私は毎朝、七時に起きます。
content.englishTranslation: I wake up at seven every morning.

content.title: One Form, More Than One Time Meaning
content.body: The Japanese non-past form does not separate the English ideas of “do” and “will do.” A frequency expression such as 毎日 usually signals a routine, while a future expression such as 明日 usually signals a plan. The verb form can stay the same; the surrounding context supplies the time meaning.

content.japaneseSentence:
毎日、日本語を勉強します。
明日も日本語を勉強します。
content.englishTranslation:
I study Japanese every day.
I will study Japanese tomorrow too.

content.title: Polite Affirmative, Negative, And Questions
content.body: Use ます to make a polite affirmative statement and ません to make a polite non-past negative statement. Add か after ます to ask a polite yes-or-no question. These endings are useful with teachers, coworkers, customers, and people you do not know well.

content.POLITE:
Affirmative: Verb stem + ます
Negative: Verb stem + ません
Question: Verb stem + ますか

content.title: Answering Polite Verb Questions
content.body: A polite verb question often repeats the same verb in the answer. For an affirmative answer, use はい and the verb ending in ます. For a negative answer, use いいえ and the verb ending in ません. Repeating the verb keeps the answer clear for beginners.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：毎日、日本語を勉強しますか。
B：はい、勉強します。
content.englishTranslation:
A: Do you study Japanese every day?
B: Yes, I do.

content.title: Keep The Verb Last, But Drop What Is Obvious
content.body: A safe beginner pattern is topic + time + place or object + verb. Japanese can also omit the topic when both speakers already know who is being discussed. In a short conversation, 明日、図書館へ行きます sounds natural without repeating 私は.

lessons.title: U Verbs And RU Verbs IN Time
lessons.learningObjective: mengonjugasi verba kelompok utama ke negatif dan lampau.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson builds on polite verb endings by showing how the two main regular verb groups form everyday sentences across time. You will learn how u-verbs and ru-verbs connect to ます, then change them into polite past and polite negative-past forms.

content.title: Two Main Regular Verb Groups
content.body: Most Japanese verbs introduced at this stage belong to one of two regular groups. U-verbs change their final dictionary-form sound before a polite ending is added. Ru-verbs usually drop the final る before the polite ending. Recognizing the group helps you build the correct form without memorizing every polite form as a separate word.

content.title: Building The Polite Stem Of U-Verbs
content.body: For an u-verb, move the final kana from its u sound to the matching i sound, then add the polite ending. For example, 書く becomes 書きます, 飲む becomes 飲みます, and 話す becomes 話します.

content.POLITE:
う → います
く → きます
ぐ → ぎます
す → します
つ → ちます
ぬ → にます
ぶ → びます
む → みます
る → ります

content.japaneseSentence:
毎晩、本を読みます。
土曜日に友達と話します。
content.englishTranslation:
I read a book every evening.
I talk with a friend on Saturday.

content.title: Building The Polite Stem Of Ru-Verbs
content.body: For a regular ru-verb, remove the final る and add the polite ending. For example, 食べる becomes 食べます, and 見る becomes 見ます. The part left after removing る stays stable when you change the time or polarity.

content.POLITE:
Ru-verb dictionary form: Verb stem + る
Polite non-past: Verb stem + ます
Example: 食べる → 食べます

content.japaneseSentence:
毎朝、七時に起きます。
夜、テレビを見ます。
content.englishTranslation:
I wake up at seven every morning.
I watch television at night.

content.title: Past Actions Use ました
content.body: To describe an action that happened and finished, keep the polite stem and replace ます with ました. The same ending works for both regular groups. A past-time expression such as 昨日, 昨夜, or 先週 makes the time reference clear.

content.POLITE:
U-verb polite stem + ました
書き + ました → 書きました
読み + ました → 読みました

Ru-verb stem + ました
食べ + ました → 食べました
見 + ました → 見ました

content.japaneseSentence:
昨日、図書館で本を読みました。
家へ帰ってから、晩ご飯を食べました。
content.englishTranslation:
Yesterday, I read a book at the library.
After returning home, I ate dinner.

content.title: Negative Past Uses ませんでした
content.body: Use ません when an action does not happen in the present or future. To say that an action did not happen in the past, use ませんでした. Keep this entire ending together: ません + でした. This pattern is the same for u-verbs and ru-verbs after their polite stems have been formed.

content.POLITE:
U-verb polite stem + ません = polite non-past negative
U-verb polite stem + ませんでした = polite negative past
行きません → 行きませんでした

Ru-verb stem + ません = polite non-past negative
Ru-verb stem + ませんでした = polite negative past
食べません → 食べませんでした

content.japaneseSentence:
昨日は学校へ行きませんでした。
朝は忙しかったですから、何も食べませんでした。
content.englishTranslation:
I did not go to school yesterday.
I did not eat anything in the morning because I was busy.

content.title: Do Not Classify A Verb By る Alone
content.body: Many ru-verbs end in an -iru or -eru sound, but not every verb ending in る belongs to the ru-verb group. For example, 食べる → 食べます is a ru-verb pattern, while 帰る → 帰ります follows the u-verb pattern. Learn the group together with each new verb when the ending could be misleading.

content.title: Use Time Expressions To Read The Ending
content.body: Verb endings and time expressions work together. 毎日 often appears with ます for a routine, while 昨日 naturally leads to ました or ませんでした. In longer sentences, find the time phrase first and then check whether the final verb confirms an affirmative or negative past action.

A：昨日、映画を見ましたか。
B：いいえ、見ませんでした。家で本を読みました。
content.englishTranslation:
A: Did you watch a movie yesterday?
B: No, I did not. I read a book at home.

lessons.title: Irregular Verbs And Purpose
lessons.learningObjective: memakai `する`, `くる`, dan purpose phrase untuk aktivitas umum.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson introduces two essential irregular verbs, する and 来る, then shows how a movement verb can explain the purpose of a trip. You will practice common polite forms such as します and 来ます, and build useful sentences such as 本を買いに行きます.

content.title: する Does Not Follow The Regular Verb Rules
content.body: する means “to do.” It is irregular, so you should learn its forms as a set instead of trying to apply the normal u-verb or ru-verb rules. In polite speech, the core forms are します, しません, しました, and しませんでした.

content.STANDARD:
する = do / will do
しない = do not / will not do
した = did
しなかった = did not do
content.POLITE:
します = do / will do
しません = do not / will not do
しました = did
しませんでした = did not do

content.japaneseSentence:
毎晩、日本語を勉強します。
昨日は運動しませんでした。
content.englishTranslation:
I study Japanese every evening.
I did not exercise yesterday.

content.title: Many Activities Use Noun + する
content.body: A large number of everyday activities are made by placing an activity noun before する. For example, 勉強する means “to study,” 運動する means “to exercise,” and 電話する means “to call.” The noun stays the same while する changes for time and politeness.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：週末は何をしますか。
B：土曜日は掃除をします。日曜日は勉強します。
content.englishTranslation:
A: What will you do this weekend?
B: I will clean on Saturday. I will study on Sunday.

content.title: 来る  Means To Come
content.body: 来る describes movement toward the speaker, the listener, or a place treated as the current point of reference. It is also irregular. Its polite forms begin with き: 来ます, 来ません, 来ました, and 来ませんでした.

content.STANDARD:
来る = come / will come
来ない = do not come / will not come
来た = came
来なかった = did not come
content.POLITE:
来ます = come / will come
来ません = do not come / will not come
来ました = came
来ませんでした = did not come

content.japaneseSentence:
友達が家に来ます。
田中さんは昨日学校に来ませんでした。
content.englishTranslation:
A friend will come to my house.
Mr. Tanaka did not come to school yesterday.

content.title: Say Why You Go Somewhere
content.body: To explain the purpose of movement, place the action before に, then finish with a movement verb such as 行きます, 来ます, or 帰ります. The action before に uses the same stem that appears before ます.

content.ALL:
Verb polite stem + に + 行く / 来る / 帰る
食べに行く = go to eat
買いに行く = go to buy
勉強しに来る = come to study
content.POLITE:
Verb polite stem + に + 行きます / 来ます / 帰ります
食べに行きます
買いに行きます
勉強しに来ます

content.japaneseSentence:
昼ご飯を食べに食堂へ行きます。
友達は日本語を勉強しに家へ来ます。
content.englishTranslation:
I go to the cafeteria to eat lunch.
My friend comes to my house to study Japanese.

content.title: Build The Purpose Form From The ます Stem
content.body: For a ru-verb, remove る: 食べる → 食べに行きます. For a u-verb, use its polite stem: 買う → 買いに行きます and 読む → 読みに行きます. For する, use し: 運動しに行きます.

content.japaneseSentence:
図書館へ本を借りに行きました。
公園へ写真を撮りに行きます。
妹は部屋へ掃除をしに来ました。
content.englishTranslation:
I went to the library to borrow a book.
I will go to the park to take pictures.
My younger sister came to the room to clean it.

content.title: Choose The Movement Verb From The Direction
content.body: The phrase before に tells the purpose, while the final movement verb tells the direction. Use 行きます when moving away toward another place, 来ます when someone comes toward the reference point, and 帰ります when returning home or to a familiar base. Read the whole situation before choosing the final verb.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：どうして学校に来ましたか。
B：先生と話しに来ました。
content.englishTranslation:
A: Why did you come to school?
B: I came to talk with the teacher.

lessons.title: Desire Intention And Invitation
lessons.learningObjective: mengekspresikan keinginan, niat, ajakan, dan pengalaman dasar.

content.title: Lesson Focus
content.body: This lesson helps you talk about what you want to do, what you intend to do, and what you would like to do together with someone else. You will also learn how to ask about past experiences with ～たことがあります. These patterns make short conversations about plans, invitations, and personal experiences much more natural.

content.title: Expressing A Personal Desire With ～たい
content.body: Use ～たい when you want to perform an action. Start with the verb form that comes before ます, then add たいです. For example, 食べます becomes 食べたいです, and 行きます becomes 行きたいです.

content.STANDARD:
Verb polite stem + たい
Verb polite stem + たくない
content.POLITE:
Verb polite stem + たいです
Verb polite stem + たくないです

content.japaneseSentence:
今日はラーメンを食べたいです。
週末に友達と映画を見たいです。
content.englishTranslation:
I want to eat ramen today.
I want to watch a movie with a friend this weekend.

content.title: Saying What You Do Not Want To Do
content.body: The negative form is ～たくないです. It is useful when declining an action or explaining a personal preference, as in 今日は出かけたくないです. At this level, use ～たいです mainly for your own desire, or in a question asking the listener what they want to do.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：休みの日に何をしたいですか。

B：家で本を読みたいです。
content.englishTranslation:
A: What do you want to do on your day off?

B: I want to read a book at home.

content.title: Stating An Intention With つもり
content.body: Use つもりです when you have already formed an intention or plan. Place the dictionary form of a verb before it: 来年、日本へ行くつもりです. To say that you intend not to do something, use the plain negative form before つもりです.

content.STANDARD:
Verb dictionary form + つもりだ
Verb plain negative + つもりだ
content.POLITE:
Verb dictionary form + つもりです
Verb plain negative + つもりです

content.japaneseSentence:
来月、新しい自転車を買うつもりです。
日曜日は仕事をしないつもりです。
content.englishTranslation:
I intend to buy a new bicycle next month.
I intend not to work on Sunday.

content.title: Making A Friendly Proposal With ～ましょう
content.body: Use ～ましょう to propose doing something together: “Let’s do it.” Replace ます with ましょう. For example, 帰ります becomes 帰りましょう.

content.POLITE:
Verb polite stem + ましょう
食べます → 食べましょう
行きます → 行きましょう
します → しましょう

content.japaneseSentence:
少し休みましょう。
授業のあとで、一緒に勉強しましょう。
content.englishTranslation:
Let’s take a short break.
Let’s study together after class.

content.title: Inviting Someone With ～ませんか
content.body: Use ～ませんか to invite someone politely: “Would you like to…?” Although the form looks negative, the whole sentence is an invitation. Replace ます with ませんか.

content.POLITE:
Verb polite stem + ませんか
飲みます → 飲みませんか
見ます → 見ませんか
きます → きませんか

content.japaneseSentence:
A：土曜日、一緒に映画を見ませんか。

B：いいですね。見ましょう。
content.englishTranslation:
A: Would you like to watch a movie together on Saturday?

B: That sounds good. Let’s watch it.

content.title: ～ましょう And ～ませんか Have Different Roles
content.body: ～ませんか gently asks whether the other person would like to join. ～ましょう makes a proposal more directly or confirms an accepted plan. A natural exchange is 一緒に行きませんか followed by はい、行きましょう.

content.title: Talking About Experience With ～たことがある
content.body: Use verb past plain form + ことがあります to say that you have done something before. The pattern focuses on whether the experience has happened at least once, not on one specific past event. Common forms include 行く → 行った, 食べる → 食べた, する → した, and くる → きた.

content.STANDARD:
Verb past plain form + ことがある
Verb past plain form + ことがない
content.POLITE:
Verb past plain form + ことがあります
Verb past plain form + ことがありません

content.japaneseSentence:
京都へ行ったことがあります。
納豆を食べたことがありません。
content.englishTranslation:
I have been to Kyoto.
I have never eaten natto.

content.japaneseSentence:
A：夏休みに何をしたいですか。

B：京都へ行きたいです。まだ行ったことがありません。

A：私も京都へ行くつもりです。一緒に行きませんか。

B：いいですね。行きましょう。
content.englishTranslation:
A: What do you want to do during summer vacation?

B: I want to go to Kyoto. I have never been there.

A: I also intend to go to Kyoto. Would you like to go together?

B: That sounds good. Let’s go.
